title: Army delays the planned detonation of old lead azide at an Iowa plant to Wednesday, 25 November
dek: The Army plans to destroy thousands of pounds of unstable explosive near a town of about 400 people, and the date has moved twice.

corrections.text: Added the 9 a.m. CST target time, the relocation of Middletown residents and NASA's data collection. The earlier text said I did not find the new evacuation hours.

what: The Army plans controlled detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, to destroy about 9,700 pounds (68 barrels) of lead azide, per ABC News. The Army's advisory of 15 November says residents will hear a loud noise, feel vibrations from two rapid detonations and see a dust plume that will contain some lead.

ABC and MPR News report the material was stored for more than 20 years in barrels of ethanol and water. The EPA, which permitted the work, said recrystallization has made it more sensitive to friction and shock, and that disturbing the containers "could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation." MPR reports the emergency permit was approved on 13 November and sets air and dust tracking and advance public notice.

The detonation was first set for Friday, 20 November, and moved to Monday, 23 November. ABC quotes Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle saying that was the latest possible moment before a forecast temperature drop that would risk further destabilization. The U.S. Army account then posted that it is now set for Wednesday, 25 November, "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."

The Army's advisory of 24 November says the detonation is planned for about 9:00 a.m. CST on Wednesday, 25 November, with exact timing to be announced after a weather check. It says a March 11, 2026 inspection found the stored lead azide had partly crystallized, and that detonating it was judged safer than chemical treatment, thermal processing, moving it or storing it longer. The Army says FEMA is supporting a recommended relocation of all residents of Middletown from Tuesday, 24 November, with transport, shelter through Friday, 27 November, and meals. The relocation zone is a 5-mile cone southwest of the plant plus a mile as a precaution. People outside it are told to shelter in place with windows closed and heating set to recirculate. NASA says it has sent research aircraft and is using its TEMPO satellite instrument to collect air data for the federal response. The Army says it will post maps starting six hours before detonation and every hour after. As of this writing, early on 25 November, I could not confirm the detonation had happened.

Residents near Middletown City Park were asked to leave for several hours, and those who could not were told to shelter indoors, per ABC. The Army projected lead dust could settle over an area about 25 miles long and 5 miles wide, per ABC. MPR reports earlier maps showed drift up to 100 miles and that some communities were later removed. The CDC says there is no safe blood lead level for children. A city official told MPR "the biggest issue we're having is the lack of information."
why: Lead dust near homes, a changing date and little detail for residents have kept the story moving.
next: The Army says exact timing follows a weather check on the morning of 25 November. Whether it went ahead, and what air monitoring shows afterwards, will be on the Army and EPA pages.
